rows.question: What is the notice period before filing a cheque bounce complaint?
queries: What is the notice period before filing a cheque bounce complaint?
dishonour of cheque notice to drawer within thirty days demand payment
Negotiable Instruments Act section 138 notice period cause of action
Negotiable Instruments Act section 142 cognizance of offences complaint
rows.answer:
(a) The payee or holder in due course must make a demand for payment by giving a notice in writing to the drawer within thirty days of receiving information from the bank that the cheque has been returned unpaid, and the drawer must fail to make the payment within fifteen days of receiving that notice [1].

Conditions and time limits:
- The cheque must be presented to the bank within six months from the date it is drawn or within its period of validity, whichever is earlier [1].
- The notice demanding payment in writing must be given by the payee or holder in due course within thirty days of receiving information from the bank that the cheque was returned as unpaid [1].
- The drawer of the cheque has a period of fifteen days from the date of receipt of the notice to make the payment [1].
- As noted in the Supreme Court judgment Kamlesh Kumar versus State of Bihar & Anr., after the cheque is returned unpaid, the notice has to be issued within thirty days of receipt of information, and fifteen days' time from the receipt of the notice must be given to the noticee to make payment [12].

rows.question: What is presumed about consideration for a negotiable instrument?
queries: What is presumed about consideration for a negotiable instrument?
presumption as to consideration for negotiable instrument
Negotiable Instruments Act section 118 presumption as to negotiable instruments
Negotiable Instruments Act section 118 holder in due course consideration
topSources: The Gujarat Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949 s1
The Portuguese Code of Civil Procedure, 1939 s2
The Himachal Pradesh Town and Country Planning Act, 1977 s?
rows.answer:
Until the contrary is proved, it shall be presumed that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated, or transferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiated, or transferred for consideration, according to Section 118 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1]. 

As discussed in the Supreme Court judgment in *K.P.O. Moideenkutty Hajee versus Pappu Manjooran and Anr.*, Section 118(a) imposes a duty on the court to raise this presumption in favour of the plaintiff once the execution of the promissory note is proved, which shifts the burden of proof to the defendant to establish that the instrument is not supported by consideration [11].

Related provisions:
- Section 43 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, which covers a negotiable instrument made, drawn, accepted, indorsed or transferred without consideration, or for a consideration which fails [10].
- Section 118 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, which covers other presumptions as to negotiable instruments such as date, time of acceptance, time of transfer, order of indorsements, stamp, and holder in due course [1].

rows.question: When can a contract be avoided if consent was obtained by coercion or misrepresentation?
queries: When can a contract be avoided if consent was obtained by coercion or misrepresentation?

rows.answer:
A contract can be avoided when consent to the agreement is caused by coercion or misrepresentation, making it a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused under Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. 

However, a contract whose consent was caused by misrepresentation or by fraudulent silence within the meaning of Section 17 is not voidable if the party whose consent was so caused had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence, as stated in Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. Furthermore, a misrepresentation that did not cause the consent of the party on whom it was made does not render the contract voidable under Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1].

rows.question: Who is competent to enter into a contract?
queries: Who is competent to enter into a contract?
capacity of persons to contract soundness of mind age of majority
Indian Contract Act section 11
Indian Contract Act section 12 mental capacity to contract
rows.answer:
- Every person who is of the age of majority according to the law to which they are subject, is of sound mind, and is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which they are subject, is competent to enter into a contract, as stated in Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1].
- Under Section 3 of the Majority Act, 1875, every person domiciled in India attains the age of majority on completing the age of eighteen years and not before [9].
- According to Section 12 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a person is of sound mind for the purpose of making a contract if, at the time of making it, they are capable of understanding it and of forming a rational judgment as to its effect upon their interests [2].
- As discussed in the Supreme Court judgment in M/S N. N. Global Mercantile Private Limited versus M/S Indo Unique Flame Ltd. & Ors., Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 declares that every person is competent to contract according to the law to which they are subject, provided they are of sound mind and not disqualified from contracting by any law [1].

rows.question: What is the punishment for murder?
queries: What is the punishment for murder?
punishment for murder causing death of person culpable homicide
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita section 103 punishment for murder
Indian Penal Code section 302 punishment for murder
topSources: The Indian Penal Code, 45 of 1860 (Rep., Act 45 of 2023) s302
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s531
rows.answer:
Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine under Section 103 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1]. 

When a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on the ground of race, caste or community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or any other similar ground, each member of such group shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine under Section 103 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1]. 

Whoever, being under sentence of imprisonment for life, commits murder, shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, which shall mean the remainder of that person's natural life under Section 104 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [5].

rows.question: What is the punishment for theft?
queries: What is the punishment for theft?
theft punishment Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita

topSources: The Indian Penal Code, 45 of 1860 (Rep., Act 45 of 2023) s379

rows.answer:
Whoever commits theft shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both, under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1]. For a second or subsequent conviction under this section, the punishment is rigorous imprisonment for a term of not less than one year up to five years, along with fine [1]. However, under the proviso to Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, if a person is convicted for the first time and the value of the stolen property is less than five thousand rupees, upon returning the value of the property or restoring the stolen property, they shall be punished with community service [1].

rows.question: What is the punishment for defamation?
queries: What is the punishment for defamation?

topSources: The Indian Penal Code, 45 of 1860 (Rep., Act 45 of 2023) s500

The Indian Penal Code, 45 of 1860 (Rep., Act 45 of 2023) s499

rows.answer:
Whoever defames another shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both, or with community service under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1]. Similarly, Section 500 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 provides that whoever defames another shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both [2][4].

Related provisions:

- Section 222 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 covers prosecution for defamation [9].
- Section 359 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 covers the compounding of offences, including defamation under Section 356(2) [5].

rows.question: When can a person accused of a non-bailable offence be released on bail?
queries: When can a person accused of a non-bailable offence be released on bail?

rows.answer:
A person accused or suspected of a non-bailable offence may be released on bail by an officer in charge of a police station, or by a Court other than the High Court or Court of Session, when arrested, detained, appearing, or brought before them [1][9][10]. 

However, such a person shall not be released on bail if there appear reasonable grounds for believing that they have been guilty of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life [1][9][10]. Additionally, they shall not be released if the offence is a cognizable offence and they have been previously convicted of an offence punishable with death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for seven years or more, or have been previously convicted on two or more occasions of a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment for three years or more but less than seven years [1][10]. 

Despite these restrictions, the Court may direct that such a person be released on bail if the person is a child or under the age of sixteen years, a woman, sick, or infirm [1][2][9][10]. rows.question: On what grounds can an arbitral award be set aside and within what time?
queries: On what grounds can an arbitral award be set aside and within what time?
application for setting aside arbitral award grounds limitation period
Arbitration and Conciliation Act section 34 application for setting aside arbitral award
Arbitration and Conciliation Act section 34 sub section 3 limitation period condonation of delay
topSources: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 s34

The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 s3
rows.answer:
An arbitral award may be set aside by the Court only on the grounds specified in Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. [1]

The Court may set aside an award if the party making the application establishes on the basis of the record of the arbitral tribunal that a party was under some incapacity, the arbitration agreement is not valid under the law, the party was not given proper notice of the appointment of an arbitrator or of the arbitral proceedings or was otherwise unable to present its case, the award deals with a dispute not contemplated by or not falling within the terms of the submission to arbitration or contains decisions on matters beyond the scope of the submission, or the composition of the arbitral tribunal or the arbitral procedure was not in accordance with the agreement of the parties or Part I of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 [1]. 

The Court may also set aside an award if it finds that the subject-matter of the dispute is not capable of settlement by arbitration under the law for the time being in force, or the arbitral award is in conflict with the public policy of India [1]. rows.question: How is a sale of immovable property defined and completed?
queries: How is a sale of immovable property defined and completed?
sale of immovable property definition and how made transfer of property
Transfer of Property Act section 54 sale how made

rows.answer:
"Sale" is defined as a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price paid or promised or part-paid and part-promised, according to Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 [1]. 

To complete a sale of tangible immovable property of the value of one hundred rupees and upwards, or a reversion or other intangible thing, it can be made only by a registered instrument, as provided in Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 [1]. In the State of Assam, such transfer must be by an instrument registered in the State of Assam, notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the Indian Registration Act, 1908, under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 [1]. For tangible immovable property of a value less than one hundred rupees, the transfer may be made either by a registered instrument or by delivery of the property, where delivery takes place when the seller places the buyer, or such person as the buyer directs, in possession of the property, pursuant to Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 [1].

rows.question: What are the inherent powers of a civil court?
queries: What are the inherent powers of a civil court?
inherent powers of court save inherent power of court to make such orders as may be necessary
Code of Civil Procedure section 151
Code of Civil Procedure saving of inherent powers of Court
topSources: The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 s151
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s528
The CODE OF CRIMINAL PROCEDURE, 1973 s477
rows.answer:
Nothing in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 shall limit or otherwise affect the inherent power of the Court to make such orders as may be necessary for the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of the process of the Court, as stated in Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 [1]. 

In the case of State of Maharashtra versus Maharau Srawan Hatkar, the Supreme Court judgment excerpt notes that Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 gives inherent power to the Court, but it is intended only to prevent abuse of the process of the court or to meet the ends of justice [1].

Related provisions:

- Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, which covers saving of inherent powers of High Court to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under this Code, or to prevent abuse of the process of any Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice [5]

rows.question: What is the punishment for identity theft using a computer?

Whoever fraudulently or dishonestly makes use of the electronic signature, password, or any other unique identification feature of any other person shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine which may extend to rupees one lakh, under Section 66C of the Information Technology Act, 2000 [1].
